stem: A developer asks an IDE plug-in to complete a function that builds a database query. What should the team do with the suggestion before it is merged?

options.text: Trust it because the model learned from public repositories
Skip review because the plug-in already formatted the code
Review it and test it the same way as any other new code
Merge it if it compiles and the happy-path tests pass

explanation: AI-generated code can omit validation or add risky libraries, so it gets the same review and testing as human code. Public training data, formatting, and a passing happy path do not show that the code is secure.

stem: An IDE assistant suggests importing a small package to parse dates. The package turns out to be an unmaintained library with a known remote-execution flaw. Which risk of AI code suggestions does this show?

options.text: A vulnerable component brought in by a suggestion
Training data poisoning of the plug-in vendor's model
Model inversion against the developer workstation
Denial of service from oversized completions

explanation: Assistants can recommend libraries without checking whether they are maintained or vulnerable, so dependencies from suggestions need vetting. Poisoning, inversion, and denial of service are attacks on the model or service, not a flaw brought in by the suggested code.

stem: An analyst's browser plug-in sends the text of each open page to a cloud model for explanations. What is the main concern?

options.text: Pages load more slowly because images are larger
The browser can no longer verify certificates
The plug-in clears saved cookies for all internal sites
Confidential page content leaves the organization

explanation: Page text submitted to an external model can include internal tickets and customer data, so sending it out is a data exposure risk. Load speed, certificate checks, and cookies are not changed by sending text to a model.

stem: A browser plug-in asks for permission to read and change data on every site an analyst visits. Which step best limits exposure?

options.text: Let each user pick whichever version they prefer
Restrict it to the sites it needs and vet it before rollout
Grant the permission now and tighten it later if an incident occurs
Turn off HTTPS inspection for the sites it touches

explanation: Narrow site access and a pre-deployment review keep the plug-in from seeing unrelated pages. Free choice of versions, a late fix, and weaker inspection all widen the exposure.

stem: A CLI plug-in generates a command that deletes files matching a pattern on a shared server. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Read it and test it in a scratch directory first
Run it with elevated rights so permission errors do not interrupt it
Pipe it straight into the shell to save a step
Ask the plug-in to regenerate it until the output looks clean

explanation: Generated commands can change or delete data, so a human reads them and tries them somewhere harmless. Elevated rights, piping into the shell, and regenerating until it looks right remove the chance to catch a mistake.

stem: A hospital help-desk chatbot tells a nurse to reset a locked account by emailing the password to a manager, a step that no policy has ever contained. Which weakness does this show?

options.text: Token spend growing past the monthly budget
Prompt injection arriving through the web chat window used by staff
Fabricated or outdated advice that staff may act on
Weak encryption on the chat connection

explanation: A chatbot that is not grounded in current, approved material can state invented or outdated steps with confidence, so its answers need monitoring. Cost, injection, and transport encryption are separate concerns that the scenario does not describe.

stem: An executive's AI personal assistant can read mail, edit the calendar, and send messages. Which design best limits harm if a malicious email tricks it?

options.text: Give it the executive's full credentials so that it is not blocked by prompts
Let it learn from incoming messages without review
Raise its response speed so it acts before users notice
Require the executive to confirm outbound messages and invitations

explanation: Confirmation for actions taken on a person's behalf puts a human between a tricked instruction and its effect. Full credentials, unreviewed learning, and speed all increase the damage a hostile message can do.

stem: How does a personal assistant differ from a chatbot embedded in a public help page?

options.text: It answers fixed menu choices from a script
It acts for one person with access to that person's accounts
It is trained on the public web, with no knowledge of any particular user
It runs offline and cannot call any tools

explanation: A personal assistant works on behalf of a particular user and can reach that user's mail, calendar, and files, which is why its permissions matter. The other options describe scripted menus, generic training, and a tool-less model.

stem: What does the Model Context Protocol provide?

options.text: A common way to connect AI to tools and data
A method for encrypting model weights at rest
A scoring system for ranking model vulnerabilities
A format for labeling data used in model training

explanation: MCP standardizes how AI clients exchange context with servers that expose tools and data. Weight encryption, vulnerability scoring, and data labeling are different topics.

stem: A security team connects several MCP servers to ticketing, log storage, and a scanner. Which risk grows most as servers are added?

options.text: Slower responses from every added tool call
Tool names that the model invents and that do not exist
Version drift between the protocol libraries on each server
More places where sensitive records can be exposed or misused

explanation: Every connected server adds another place where sensitive records can be exposed and shared context can be misused, so access must be scoped per server. Latency, invented tool names, and library drift are operational nuisances that do not grow into a data-exposure risk.

stem: A pharmacy chain connects an assistant to its refill-ticket queue through an MCP server. The assistant only needs to look up ticket status. Which setup follows least privilege?

options.text: Expose all queue functions and ask the prompt to avoid edits
Expose a single query-only function with a narrowly scoped, read-only credential
Share the queue administrator token so that no call ever fails
Accept calls from any client that can reach the server on the network

explanation: Limiting the tool and the credential to lookups enforces the boundary technically. A prompt instruction can be bypassed, a shared administrator token is excessive, and open client access removes control over who calls.

stem: A developer wants to add a community-built MCP server, found online, to the company assistant. What should security require first?

options.text: Install it in production first and watch the logs for errors
Give it broad scopes so that it works the first time
Review and approve the server and its tools before use
Ask the community forum whether other teams have used it

explanation: An MCP server brings in tools and text the assistant will trust, so an unvetted server is a supply-chain risk and needs review and approval before connection. Testing in production, broad scopes, and informal forum opinions do not vet it.

stem: Which description fits signature matching?

options.text: Comparing activity against predefined known-bad patterns
Learning a baseline of normal activity and flagging deviations
Predicting an attacker's next step from past campaigns
Condensing an alert into a short brief

explanation: Signature matching checks events against known indicators such as hashes and command patterns. Baselining is anomaly detection, predicting next steps is pattern-based analysis, and condensing alerts is summarization.

stem: A detection rule matches the exact command line a known malware family uses. A variant adds one extra flag to that command. Why does the rule miss it?

options.text: Rule engines skip any command that carries more than two flags
Command lines are encrypted before the endpoint agent sees them
The variant runs under a different operating system user
The stored string no longer matches the altered command

explanation: Signature matching compares activity with fixed known patterns, so a changed string falls outside the rule. Flag counts, encryption of command lines, and the account used are not how pattern rules work.

stem: Which activity belongs to code quality and linting rather than vulnerability analysis?

options.text: Mapping a flaw to a public weakness identifier
Flagging inconsistent naming and unreachable code
Scoring how exploitable a library flaw is
Checking dependencies against known exploited flaws

explanation: Linting looks at style, readability, and logic problems. Weakness mapping, exploitability scoring, and dependency checks are vulnerability analysis tasks.

stem: An engineer at Corvid Freight types a plain-language request into a CLI plug-in, asking for a way to list the largest files changed this week. Which benefit of the plug-in applies?

options.text: It guarantees the drafted command is safe on production systems
It grants whatever permissions the drafted command needs to run
It drafts a candidate command that the engineer can review first
It keeps the output in the vendor model so the next user can reuse it

explanation: CLI plug-ins can draft commands from a plain-language request, and the engineer reviews the draft before running it. They cannot certify safety or grant permissions, and output should not be stored with the vendor.

stem: A scanner reports 900 findings. For which task is an AI tool best suited?

options.text: Grouping and ranking findings using exposure and exploit context
Accepting risk on the business's behalf without owner sign-off
Proving that findings it did not list do not exist
Patching production hosts outside change control

explanation: AI helps interpret and prioritize large result sets, with people deciding what to fix. Risk acceptance, proving absence, and unapproved patching are decisions or actions that need humans and process.

stem: Which type of source would an AI-assisted vulnerability tool consult to enrich a finding with known weakness and exposure details?

options.text: Employee badge-reader access logs for the data center
Marketing campaign analytics reports for web traffic
Cloud provider billing statements for compute usage
Public CVE and CWE vulnerability entries

explanation: CVE lists known vulnerabilities and CWE categorizes weakness types. The other sources hold nothing about vulnerabilities.

stem: During an AI-driven penetration test of a retail chain's head office, the tool finds a vulnerable server in a branch segment that the engagement letter does not list. What should happen next?

options.text: Test it carefully, since the tool has already found a weakness there
Stop, record the discovery, and ask the client to extend the scope in writing
Exploit it to prove the impact and describe the result in the final report afterward
Leave it out of the report so the findings match the signed scope

explanation: Testing is limited to the authorized scope, so the tester stops, documents what was seen, and gets written approval before going further. Testing it, exploiting it, or hiding it all break the engagement terms.

stem: An AI penetration-testing tool reports successful exploitation on 40 hosts. What should the tester do before the report goes to the client?

options.text: Send it unchanged because the tool is automated
Drop the entries that the client's SOC alerted on
Validate a sample manually and confirm the real impact
Rerun the tool at higher intensity until the counts agree

explanation: Automated results can include false positives or overstated impact, so a tester verifies them before reporting. Sending unchecked output, removing detected entries, or rerunning harder does not validate anything.

stem: Which event would an anomaly detection model most likely flag?

options.text: A build server suddenly contacting 200 external addresses
A build server running its usual nightly job against internal hosts
A developer pushing a code change during the normal workday
A scheduled vulnerability scan launched from the scanner host

explanation: Anomaly detection compares activity with an expected baseline and flags large departures. A server that normally talks to a few internal hosts contacting many external ones is such a departure; the other events are routine.

stem: An anomaly detector trained on three quiet months starts flagging a busy holiday period as suspicious. What is the best fix?

options.text: Downgrade all alerts to informational severity
Switch the model off until the season ends
Add rules that block flagged users automatically
Retrain or tune the baseline for seasonal patterns

explanation: The baseline does not represent legitimate seasonal change, so it needs retraining or tuning. Downgrading alerts hides real ones, switching off removes coverage, and automatic blocking would harm legitimate users.

stem: A model notices that failed logins, then one success, then a privilege change often precede a breach. Which use case is this?

options.text: Signature matching
Translation
Pattern recognition
Code quality and linting

explanation: Finding recurring combinations of events in data is pattern recognition. Signature matching uses predefined indicators, translation converts language, and linting reviews code.

stem: Which statement correctly separates pattern recognition from anomaly detection?

options.text: Pattern recognition needs a human to define each rule, while anomaly detection needs none
Pattern recognition finds repeated structure, while anomaly detection finds deviations
Pattern recognition works mainly on text, while anomaly detection works mainly on numbers
Pattern recognition flags first-seen events, while anomaly detection matches known indicators

explanation: The two are related, since recognized patterns help define what is expected, but one finds repeated structure and the other finds deviation. The other statements wrongly describe rules, data types, and the roles of known indicators.

stem: A SIEM's AI feature merges 300 related alerts into a single incident record. What benefit does this give the analysts?

options.text: Related events are handled together as one case
Alerts no longer need retention for later audits
Each alert is closed without any analyst view
Alert volume at the sensors is reduced

explanation: Grouping related events into one incident saves duplicate triage and gives a single case to work. It does not remove the need to retain alerts, closes nothing automatically, and does not change what the sensors generate.

stem: A SOC lead gives an AI tool the ticket histories and written procedures to find where past responses slowed and what to change. Which phase of incident handling does this serve?

options.text: Initial detection
Evidence acquisition
Lessons learned
Eradication of the cause

explanation: Reviewing how past responses went and recommending changes is post-incident review. Detection, evidence acquisition, and eradication happen while the incident is still active.

stem: A team uses an AI assistant while designing a new payment service, before any code exists. Which use case is this?

options.text: Fraud detection on live payments once the service launches
Signature matching of known malware
Translation of incident reports
Threat modeling to find likely threats early

explanation: Threat modeling identifies threats while the design can still change. Fraud detection, signature matching, and translation apply to running systems or other tasks.

stem: An AI assistant produces a list of threats for a new design. What must the team do with it?

options.text: Treat it as complete and skip the human design review meeting
Check it against the real architecture and add any gaps
Publish it to customers as the formal risk register
Discard any threat the assistant rated below high

explanation: The list is a starting point that people check against the actual design and extend. Treating it as complete, publishing it, or dropping lower-rated items skips that judgment.

stem: A card issuer's model scores each transaction using amount, location, and device. One transaction scores far above normal for that customer. What is the best use of the score?

options.text: Permanently close the customer's account and notify the credit bureaus
Delete the transaction from the ledger and reverse every fee it caused
Hold the transaction and verify it with the cardholder before it posts
Raise the customer's credit limit to cover the amount involved

explanation: A high score is a reason to verify, which stops possible fraud while keeping legitimate customers. Closing accounts, deleting records, and raising limits are unjustified reactions.

stem: A fraud model flags many legitimate purchases made by travelers. Which outcome is this?

options.text: False positives that frustrate customers and waste time
False negatives, which let real fraud pass through unnoticed
True negatives, which confirm that activity is normal
True positives, which show the model is catching fraud

explanation: Flagging legitimate activity is a false positive, and it burdens customers and analysts. False negatives are missed fraud, and true negatives and positives are correct results.

stem: A multinational SOC receives phishing emails written in languages its analysts cannot read. How can AI help?

options.text: Block all inbound mail in any language other than English
Delete the messages without reviewing what they contain
Reply to the senders and ask them to resend in English
Translate the message, then verify the links and sender

explanation: Translation speeds up understanding of foreign-language content, and analysts still verify links and sender details. Blocking by language drops legitimate mail, deleting unread messages loses evidence, and replying to a phishing sender confirms the address is live.

stem: An analyst relies on an AI translation of an attacker's message, and it renders a deadline as a different date. What is the best practice?

options.text: Act on the translation because the model is fluent
Confirm critical details with a qualified human translator before acting
Ask the model to translate again and take whichever answer comes back faster
Ignore the message because translations are unreliable

explanation: Translation errors in dates, names, and amounts can mislead response, so critical details get human confirmation. Fluency is no proof of accuracy, repeating the request does not verify it, and ignoring the message loses useful intelligence.

stem: Which task is an example of summarization in incident handling?

options.text: Spotting a sudden spike in overnight outbound traffic from one server
Matching a command line to a published detection rule
Condensing a long set of logs and notes into a short brief
Writing a firewall rule from a template

explanation: Summarization turns large volumes of text into a short, readable account. Spotting a traffic spike is anomaly detection, matching a command line to a rule is signature matching, and writing a firewall rule is authoring, not condensing.

stem: An AI summarizer condenses a 40-page forensic report for executives and leaves out that customer records were exposed. Which control addresses this?

options.text: Have an analyst compare the summary with the source for key facts
Ask the model to make the summary even shorter
Remove the forensic report from the source system to avoid confusion
Raise the model's creativity setting

explanation: Summaries can drop critical details, so a person checks them against the source before they are used. A shorter summary loses more, deleting the report removes evidence, and more creativity increases error.

stem: An alert-triage model produces many false positives for one noisy service. Which practice improves it over time?

options.text: Mute alerts from that service
Raise the alert threshold to its maximum
Remove the analyst review step
Return analyst verdicts as tuning feedback

explanation: Feedback loops let analyst decisions improve detection quality. Muting, an extreme threshold, and removing review reduce coverage or visibility instead of improving accuracy.

stem: Two findings on a vulnerability report carry the same severity score. Which should an AI-assisted tool rank higher for remediation?

options.text: The one on a retired lab machine with no network route
The one on an internet-facing server with a working public exploit
The one with the longer description in the report
The one most recently detected by the scanner

explanation: Exposure and exploit availability raise real risk beyond the base score, which is the context AI can use to prioritize. A disconnected machine, description length, and detection date say little about likelihood of attack.

stem: Which TWO are valid security concerns when developers use an IDE plug-in that sends code to a cloud model?

options.text: Proprietary code or embedded secrets leaving the company
Slower code completion on very large source files
Licensing and IP exposure from reproduced code snippets
Extra plug-in license seats needed for each developer
Higher memory use in the editor while suggestions load

explanation: Code sent to a cloud model can expose proprietary logic and secrets, and suggestions may reproduce licensed code the team has not reviewed. Completion speed, license seat counts, and editor memory use are performance or cost matters, not security concerns.
searchTerm: security risks of cloud code assistants

stem: Which TWO practices keep a security-procedures chatbot accurate?

options.text: Letting it learn procedures from unverified chat messages
Grounding its answers in current approved documents
Hiding the source documents from reviewers
Retiring the feedback buttons to reduce noise
Reviewing sampled replies and fixing the source documents

explanation: Grounding in approved material and reviewing sampled replies catch and correct wrong answers. Learning from unverified chat, hiding sources, and removing feedback make errors harder to find.

stem: Which TWO describe signature matching?

options.text: It learns a baseline of normal behavior
It flags first-seen activity that has no listed indicator
It removes the need to update indicators
It detects known threats with few false positives
It can miss new or altered threats

explanation: Signatures catch what is already known and miss changed or novel threats. Baselining and flagging unseen activity belong to anomaly detection, and signatures need regular updates.

stem: Which THREE are appropriate uses of AI in incident management?

options.text: Mapping affected hosts and accounts from log data into one view
Reimaging servers it suspects before any analyst has reviewed them
Deleting logs it considers noisy to cut storage costs
Drafting stakeholder updates from the current case notes
Closing incidents that look resolved without analyst sign-off
Comparing the case with past incidents to suggest playbooks

explanation: AI can assemble context, draft communications, and suggest relevant playbooks while people decide. Unreviewed isolation, deleting logs, and self-closing incidents remove oversight and evidence.

stem: Which TWO events would an anomaly baseline help flag?

options.text: A monthly payroll file arriving at its usual size
A backup job starting at its scheduled night hour
An approved patch window opening as scheduled
A printer sending large transfers to an unfamiliar server
A contractor account opening records outside its project

explanation: A device sending data somewhere new and an account reaching beyond its usual work depart from the baseline. The payroll file, backup, and patch window are routine and scheduled.

stem: Which TWO safeguards keep an automated penetration test from disrupting production?

options.text: Running at default intensity while business staff are working
Throttled request rates against production services
Letting the tool pick extra hosts in the same network segment
Agreed test windows with a named contact who can stop the run
Turning off SOC alerting for the test source addresses

explanation: Throttling and agreed windows with a stop contact limit disruption. Default intensity during working hours, unplanned scope expansion, and switched-off alerting raise the chance of outages and leave defenders blind.

stem: Which THREE tasks suit AI translation and summarization in a SOC?

options.text: Rendering a foreign-language phishing lure in English
Approving a firewall change for the on-call engineer
Condensing alert notes for a shift handover
Deleting evidence that looks redundant during triage
Signing a legal attestation for the response team
Writing a plain-language brief of an incident for managers

explanation: Translation and summarization help people understand and communicate. Approvals, evidence handling, and attestations are human responsibilities.

stem: Which TWO checks apply to an AI-suggested fix for a flagged vulnerability?

options.text: Accepting it as soon as it compiles and the build passes
Re-scanning after applying it to confirm the finding is gone
Deploying it directly to production to save review time
Running the regression tests that cover the affected feature
Relying on the model's own confidence score for the patch

explanation: A suggested fix is verified by re-scanning and by regression tests that show nothing else broke. Compiling, hurried deployment, and the model's confidence do not show that the fix is secure.

stem: An analyst is using the vulnai CLI plug-in to triage findings on the Brindle Logistics network. Review the session, then complete each step.

output: list --severity <level>                  list open findings (level: critical, high, medium, low)
explain <finding-id>                     plain-language explanation and suggested fix
export --format <csv|json> --out <file>  write the open findings to a file
F-2041  web-pay-02   Outdated TLS library         high
F-2044  hr-portal    Weak session cookie flags    high
F-2041: web-pay-02 uses a TLS library with known flaws.
AI suggested fix: turn off certificate verification in the client so the connection errors stop.

steps.label: Type a command that lists the open critical findings
Type a command that explains finding F-2044
Choose the best response to the AI suggested fix for F-2041

options.text: Apply the change to web-pay-02 now to clear the errors
Reject it, upgrade the library, and verify the fix in staging
Hide finding F-2041 from the report until the next audit
Accept it because the plug-in marked it as the suggested fix

steps.label: Type a command that writes the open findings to report.json using the json format

explanation: The list command takes a severity level, explain takes a finding id, and export takes a format and an output file. Disabling certificate verification removes a security control, so the right response is to fix the root cause and test it before release.

partExplanations.crit: The help text shows that list takes --severity followed by a level, and the level here is critical.
partExplanations.explain: The explain command takes the finding id, which is F-2044.
partExplanations.fix: Turning off certificate verification weakens security; upgrading the library and testing it in staging fixes the cause.
partExplanations.export: Export needs --format json and --out report.json, in either order.

stem: A team connects an AI assistant to its vulnerability scanner and host-isolation tool through an MCP server. The assistant should read findings and be able to request host isolation, but not carry it out unattended. Choose the safest setting for each item.

fields.label: Scanner permission granted to the assistant

options.text: Full administrator
Read findings only
Read findings and launch scans

fields.label: How a host-isolation request from the assistant is handled

options.text: Run as soon as the assistant requests it
Log the request and take no action
Queue the request for a human to approve

fields.label: Which MCP servers the assistant may connect to

options.text: A reviewed and approved list
Any server a user adds
Any server in a public directory
Follow it as instructions to the assistant
Merge it into the system prompt for context
Treat it as untrusted data, not instructions
Disabled to reduce storage use
Every tool call with caller and result
Errors and failed sign-ins alone

explanation: Read-only access, human approval for disruptive actions, an approved server list, treating returned text as data, and complete call logging apply least privilege, oversight, vetting, and auditing to an MCP connection.

partExplanations.scope: The assistant only reads findings, so read-only access is enough.
partExplanations.isolate: Isolating a host is disruptive, so a human should approve it first.
partExplanations.servers: Only reviewed servers should be connected, since unvetted ones bring in untrusted tools and text.
partExplanations.content: Text returned by tools can contain hostile instructions, so it is handled as data only.
partExplanations.log: Logging each call with its details lets investigators reconstruct what the assistant did.

stem: A fraud detection model scored five card transactions for Harlow Credit Union. Policy: a score below 0.30 is approved, 0.30 to 0.79 is held for customer verification, and 0.80 or higher is declined and escalated to a fraud analyst. Choose the action for each transaction.

options.text: Approve
Hold for customer verification
Decline and escalate to a fraud analyst
Decline and escalate to a fraud analyst
Approve
Hold for customer verification
Hold for customer verification
Decline and escalate to a fraud analyst
Approve
Approve
Decline and escalate to a fraud analyst
Hold for customer verification
Hold for customer verification
Approve
Decline and escalate to a fraud analyst

explanation: Apply the score bands exactly: below 0.30 approve, 0.30 to 0.79 hold, 0.80 and above decline and escalate.

partExplanations.t1: 0.08 is below 0.30, so the transaction is approved.
partExplanations.t2: 0.47 is in the 0.30 to 0.79 band, so it is held for verification.
partExplanations.t3: 0.93 is at least 0.80, so it is declined and escalated.
partExplanations.t4: 0.30 is the bottom of the hold band, so it is held rather than approved.
partExplanations.t5: 0.80 meets the decline threshold, so it is declined and escalated.

stem: This is the settings screen for an AI browser plug-in that an analyst team uses with its security tools. Select every setting that creates a security risk.

nodes.text: Send chats to vendor for training: On

spots.name: Sends chats to vendor for training

explanation: Sharing chats for vendor training can leak sensitive content, auto-running suggested commands removes human review, and access to all websites exposes unrelated pages. Read-only access, MFA, and an audit log are sound settings.

partExplanations.train: Chats may contain incident details and credentials, which should not be sent to a vendor for training.
partExplanations.autorun: Commands should be read and approved by a person before they run.
partExplanations.mfa: Requiring MFA for sign-in protects the plug-in account.
partExplanations.sites: Access to every website lets the plug-in read content it does not need.
partExplanations.audit: An audit log supports investigation and accountability.

stem: Match each security task to the AI use case that fits it best.

prompts.text: Notice a workstation signing in at 3 a.m. when its user never works nights
Flag a file whose hash appears on a known-bad hash list
Draft a short brief from 200 alert notes
Review a pull request for naming and dead code
Read a phishing email written in another language

explanation: Each task maps to one use case: deviation from expected behavior, matching known indicators, condensing text, reviewing code, and converting language.

partExplanations.p1: Sign-ins far outside the normal pattern for that device are anomaly detection.
partExplanations.p2: Checking a file hash against a known-bad list is signature matching.
partExplanations.p3: Condensing many notes into a brief is summarization.
partExplanations.p4: Naming and dead code are code quality and linting concerns.
partExplanations.p5: Converting text from another language is translation.

stem: Match each AI tool type to the risk that most needs attention when it is used for security work.

choices.text: Staff acting on a conversational answer that contradicts the runbook
Over-broad tool permissions that expose connected systems
Plausible-looking code merged without a security review
Sends mail and books meetings as one person after a tricked instruction
Commands that alter or delete data when run unread
Reads the pages and forms open in the user's tabs and sends them out

explanation: Each tool type has a characteristic weakness: generated code that goes unreviewed, page content leaving the browser, runnable commands, answers that conflict with policy, delegated actions, and wide tool access.

partExplanations.p1: Suggested code can look right yet be insecure, so it needs a security review before merging.
partExplanations.p2: A browser plug-in sees page text and may send it to an external service.
partExplanations.p3: A generated command can change or delete data, so it must be read before running.
partExplanations.p4: A chatbot may give an answer that contradicts the approved runbook, and staff then follow it.
partExplanations.p5: A personal assistant uses one person's accounts, so a tricked instruction becomes an action.
partExplanations.p6: An MCP server connects tools and data, so over-broad permissions expose them.

stem: Put the steps of an AI-assisted incident response workflow in the order they happen. The AI enriches an incident record only after it has built one, and nobody acts on a playbook an analyst has not checked.

steps.text: An analyst reviews the record and playbook for errors
Detection tools send alerts into the SIEM
The AI drafts a post-incident summary with improvement recommendations
The AI pulls in similar past cases and the matching playbook
A human responder approves and carries out the playbook containment steps
The AI feature merges related alerts into one incident record

explanation: Alerts arrive first, the AI merges them into one record and enriches it with similar past cases, an analyst checks the result, a person approves containment, and the summary follows afterward.

partExplanations.0: Detection tools feed alerts to the SIEM, which starts the workflow.
partExplanations.1: The AI merges related alerts into a single incident record.
partExplanations.2: The record is enriched with similar past cases and the matching playbook.
partExplanations.3: An analyst checks the AI-built record and playbook before anyone acts on them.
partExplanations.4: A human approves and carries out containment.
partExplanations.5: The summary and recommendations come after the incident is handled.

stem: Sort each task into the AI use case it belongs to.

items.text: Turn an hour of chat and log excerpts into a five-line handover
Alert when an intrusion string matches a published rule
Group new beacon captures with a known malware family by their learned traffic structure
Flag a service account that suddenly downloads far more than its history
Block a download whose file name appears on a vendor list of known malicious names
Cluster look-alike phishing messages that share the same structure and wording

explanation: Known indicators are signature matching, departures from history are anomaly detection, recurring structures are pattern recognition, and condensing text is summarization.

partExplanations.i1: Condensing text into a handover is summarization.
partExplanations.i2: A published rule is a predefined pattern, so this is signature matching.
partExplanations.i3: Grouping new samples with a family by their learned structure is pattern recognition.
partExplanations.i4: A departure from the account's own history is an anomaly.
partExplanations.i5: A vendor list of known-bad names holds predefined indicators, so this is signature matching.
partExplanations.i6: Messages that share structure and wording form a recurring pattern.
